relations.py:84-107 _called_names tokenizes under the dialect and, for each token followed by L_PAREN, collects VAR/IDENTIFIER tokens or tokens whose upper text is in the dialect KEYWORDS (so IN, DECIMAL are collected, per docstring 89-90); a schema prefix is not part of the token, so only the name directly before ( is collected, matching 'with or without schema. prefix'. Crafted input schema.fn( or "Fn"( or replace( traced: all collected. Lookup at 238-270 is one cursor.execute per statement (call at 133): PostgreSQL pg_proc join pg_namespace with nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema'), case-insensitive via lower(); MySQL information_schema.ROUTINES with ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION' and LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME). Doc at row-level-security.md:47 matches. The rejection concerns a test, not this doc claim.

The doc text is at row-level-security.md:45. relations.py:181-205 selects c.relkind, nspname, relname plus EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM pg_catalog.pg_inherits i WHERE i.inhrelid = c.oid) for to_regclass(name). For base-table kinds, a True flag raises RlsError, with no check of rules, so it applies whether or not a rule names the table or its parent. Each partition or inheritance child at any depth has its own pg_inherits row, so every depth is refused. A top-level table has no row and is not refused, so it still runs. A non-bool flag raises TypeError and the caller treats it as a failed lookup. Trace of a crafted input (a depth-2 child): it has its own inhrelid row, so it is refused.

Doc text is at row-level-security.md:45 (source_line 123 is stale). apply_rls (src/sqllens/safety/rls.py:205-332) has no partition special-casing. It takes base tables from scope.sources.values() that are exp.Table (282-284), and filters any whose .name is protected (286-297). In sqlglot's MySQL parser, `orders PARTITION (p0)` is parsed as one exp.Table named orders with a `partition` arg, not a separate node. So the table is a normal base-table source and gets the predicate, and the backstop at 308-330 is satisfied. I did not run sqlglot, so the parse behavior comes from my knowledge of the library, not an executed check. The SQLite statement is a general fact about SQLite and is not contradicted by the code. The rejection line is about an unrelated test and does not cover this claim.

docs/external/row-level-security.md:164 says a multi-parent child is readable through each parent, so each parent needs its own rule. src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:183-203 queries pg_inherits with i.inhrelid = c.oid for the referenced relation only, so it refuses a relation that is itself a child. It does not look at parents. A parent that names no rule therefore stays queryable, and PostgreSQL returns rows from all its children, including the multi-parent child. A rule on only one parent would leave the other as an unfiltered path, so the doc advice is accurate. I traced the falsifying input, a multi-parent child queried through an unruled parent. It supports the doc rather than breaking it.

docs/external/row-level-security.md:164 states the gap. _called_names (src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:98-106) collects a token only when the next token is L_PAREN, so `o.order_total` with no parentheses is not collected. The doc's description of the check and of PostgreSQL attribute notation (o.col resolving to function col(rel)) is accurate. The rejection line concerns an unrelated MySQL test and does not apply.

relations.py:181-188 selects relkind, nspname, relname, EXISTS(...) so the flag is row[3] (used at line 194). An EXISTS expression has SQL type boolean, which psycopg2's default typecaster (OID 16) returns as Python bool, so isinstance(is_child, bool) passes at line 195. pg_inherits.inhrelid holds the child OID for both partitions and INHERITS children. The rejection line concerns a MySQL test and does not cover this claim. This rests on psycopg2's documented behavior; I did not run it.

relations.py:182-205 uses EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM pg_inherits WHERE inhrelid = c.oid). Per PostgreSQL docs, pg_inherits has a row (inhrelid=child, inhparent=direct parent) for each direct child, created by both INHERITS and PARTITION OF. In multi-level hierarchies every non-root table is a direct child of its parent, so each has a row. A top-level table has no row as inhrelid. The rejection line concerns an unrelated MySQL test and does not cover this claim.

relations.py:248-255 passes (names, names) as parameters with proname::text = ANY(%s) and lower(proname::text) = ANY(%s). The Postgres runner (sql_runner.py:61-65,171) uses psycopg2 and passes its plain conn to verify_base_tables. psycopg2 adapts a non-empty list[str] to ARRAY['a','b'], which Postgres types as text[], so text = ANY(text[]) is valid and raises no cast error. This is documented psycopg2 behavior. I did not run it against a live server. The rejection line concerns the MySQL test and does not apply.

The MySQL runner connects via PyMySQL (sql_runner.py:51,107), whose paramstyle is 'format' (%s). relations.py:257-263 builds one %s per name and passes tuple(names), so the placeholder count matches the argument count. The guard `if called:` at relations.py:132 means _refuse_database_routines runs only with a non-empty list, so the placeholder list is never empty. The sorted list from _called_names is a list of str. The cursor comes from connection.cursor() (default tuple cursor), so row[0] works.

relations.py:258-263 queries information_schema.ROUTINES with ROUTINE_NAME and ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION', both real MySQL columns (ROUTINE_TYPE is FUNCTION or PROCEDURE). The visibility claim rests on my recollection of the MySQL docs, which I did not re-read: rows appear for routines the user may execute or has other routine privileges on (EXECUTE, ALTER ROUTINE, SHOW_ROUTINE, or definer), not only ones it created. A function the user cannot see is one it cannot call, so the lookup covers what matters. The rejection line concerns test column coverage, not this claim, and the repository's connector tests reportedly exercise the real lookup.

relations.py:97-107 _called_names returns {text, text.lower(), ascii_lower}; relations.py:257-263 MySQL arm uses LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (names). A mixed-case stored name is lowered by LOWER(), so only the lower-cased candidate (equal to the ASCII-lowered one for ASCII names) can match; the as-written mixed-case candidate cannot. Matches the claim. The rejection line concerns a test fake's column and is unrelated.

relations.py:128-135 creates one plain connection.cursor() and runs _verify_relations (lines 158-235) then _refuse_database_routines (238-270) sequentially, closing in finally. Each lookup does execute then fetchone. The connection is created without cursorclass or cursor_factory (grep of integrations), so the cursor is a default buffered one: psycopg2 client-side and pymysql Cursor. The next execute on it is safe. The streaming cursors (postgres sql_runner.py:177 named cursor, mysql sql_runner.py:149 SSDictCursor) are made only after verify_base_tables returns (mysql :140 before :149; postgres :170 before :177), and are separate cursors. The MySQL @@lower_case_table_names fetchone happens on the same buffered cursor before the relation loop. The rejection line concerns a test column, not this claim.

relations.py:94-107: for any token followed by L_PAREN, it is collected if VAR/IDENTIFIER or if token.text.upper() is in the dialect tokenizer's KEYWORDS (sqlglot base KEYWORDS include IN and DECIMAL, inherited by postgres/mysql). Each collected text adds (text, text.lower(), ASCII-only lower) to a set, so the three forms are returned (duplicates collapse, which is still consistent with the docstring). I did not run the tokenizer; this rests on reading the loop and on my knowledge of sqlglot's keyword table. Traced input: `x IN (1)` and `DECIMAL(5,2)` both reach the keyword branch. The rejection line concerns a different test and does not cover this item.

relations.py:125-133 runs the routine check when a call name exists even with no relations (early return only if both empty). _called_names (84-107) returns the written, lower() and ASCII-only-lower forms of each VAR/IDENTIFIER/keyword token before '('. PostgreSQL predicate (252) matches proname exactly or lower(proname) against those names. A mixed-case or uppercase proname matches a call in any case, and a non-ASCII proname matches through the ASCII-lower form when the server does not fold. MySQL (261) uses LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (names) restricted to FUNCTION. Only obscure Unicode special-case lowering such as U+0130 might differ, which does not break the claimed behaviour. The rejection line concerns test coverage and is not relied on.

criteria.json counts (criterion 1 matches). relations.py:181-205: postgres lookup selects EXISTS(pg_inherits where inhrelid=c.oid); for relkind r/p, a bool True raises RlsError 'partition and inheritance child tables...'; non-bool raises TypeError -> sanitized RlsError (138-155). inhrelid covers PARTITION OF and INHERITS at any depth, independent of rules (check is rule-independent). _relations (61-81) uses traverse_scope over all scopes (FROM, join, subquery, CTE) and raises on any unaccounted exp.Table, so no position escapes. verify_base_tables is called in postgres sql_runner.py:171 before execution. Parent: not a child, passes; rule rewrite scopes it; connector test test_connectors.py:212-217 asserts parent returns [1,3] (including inheritance-child rows), partition and child blocked even when rules name them (line 207). Trigger alternatives: kind v/m/other -> view/unverifiable refusal (still refusal, outside the criterion's trigger as not a child base table); metadata-view continue -> system views are not children (outside trigger); row None -> refused fail-closed; lookup exception -> sanitized RlsError (fails closed).

criteria.json read, criterion 2 present and valid. relations.py:84-107 _called_names tokenizes the SQL (not typed nodes) and collects every token before L_PAREN that is VAR/IDENTIFIER or a dialect keyword (so replace, position, strpos-as-emitted are covered), with exact, lower and ASCII-lower variants; schema-qualified calls work because only the last token before '(' is taken. verify_base_tables (110-135) runs it for postgres/mysql regardless of relations (line 126 returns only when no relations AND no called names), so relation-free statements are checked. _refuse_database_routines (238-270): PG queries pg_proc excluding pg_catalog/information_schema, matching on proname alone (no schema/signature filter, extension functions included); MySQL queries information_schema.ROUTINES FUNCTION with LOWER(name) match; any row raises RlsError. Runners call verify_base_tables(conn, args.sql) (postgres sql_runner.py:171, mysql sql_runner.py:140) on the SQL the runner receives, i.e. the post-rewrite SQL; test at test_rls_views.py:618-628 applies apply_rls then verifies, asserting the executed name (strpos/position) is looked up. Tokens are position-independent so select list, FROM, joins, filters, aggregates, windows are all covered. Split conditions: 'if not relations and not called' -> outside the trigger (no call names, so no call to refuse); 'dialect in (postgres,mysql)' else [] -> sqlite, outside trigger (criterion names PG/MySQL only); token filter 'not token.text' / non-VAR-IDENT-keyword token before '(' -> not a call name (e.g. string/number), outside trigger; lookup exceptions -> caught at 138-155 and fail closed with RlsError (sibling criterion 6). read_only independence: the check is in the runner path gated by require_base_tables, not by read_only.

criteria.json read; criterion 3 present, graded with it. With no rules the branch is skipped, so behavior is unchanged.
